items.title: Satya Niketan building collapse: Delhi HC seeks response from DU, Centre, State on PIL for hostels in all colleges
items.summary: The Delhi High Court on Wednesday issued notice to Delhi University, Delhi government and the Central government on a public interest litigation (PIL) petition seeking directions to ensure that each and every college affiliated to DU has hostel facilities for students. A Division Bench of Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia directed the respondents to file their replies, adding that the case will be heard next on September 15. The PIL was filed after a paying guest (PG) building in Delhi's Satya Niketan caved in, leading to the death of 7 including students. The Court said that the matter will be heard with other PILs related to the collapse of Satya Niketan building. Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia The PIL was filed by one Vinod Jakhar seeking directions to address the acute shortage of safe, affordable and adequate hostel accommodation for students of DU and its colleges. It stated that Delhi University was established in 1922 as a “teaching and residential University" but its hostel infrastructure has failed to keep pace with its expansion. Around 1.32 lakh students are enrolled in regular programmes, while several colleges either have no hostel facilities or have severely limited capacity. Therefore, the PIL has sought a college-wise assessment of hostel requirements, a time-bound University-wide hostel development policy, cluster hostels where land is unavailable, and structural and fire-safety audits of private PGs and student hostels. Advocates Rishav Ranjan, Vimal Tyagi and Balaji Pathak appeared for Vinod Jakhar. Solicitor General (SG) Tushar Mehta , Additional Solicitor General (ASG) Chetan Sharma with Central Government Standing Counsels (CGSC) Jagdish Chandra and Nishant Gautam appeared for the Central government. items.title: Pallikaranai Collective’s charter seeks coordinated action to protect wetlands
items.summary: Follow TNM’s WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. There should be coordinated government action to protect wetlands and reduce flooding in the Pallikaranai watershed, said the ‘Citizen’s Charter for Pallikaranai Watershed’, compiled by the Chennai Wetlands Action Collective (CWAC) and Oorvani Foundation, with the Federation of OMR Residents Associations (FOMRRA). The charter was released by the Pallikaranai Collective, a body of resident welfare associations, conservation groups, civil society organisations, activists, and citizens, on Wednesday, September 9. The concerns and recommendations listed in the charter were discussed at the Chennai Press Club on Thursday, September 10. It highlighted that Chennai is a rapidly growing city, which has witnessed severe flooding, recurring water scarcity, extreme heat, and contamination of drinking water. The degradation of the wetlands has increased the vulnerability of the city. The Pallikaranai watershed is one of Chennai’s most flood-prone and rapidly urbanising regions. According to the charter, the watershed covers 65 major lakes and hundreds of ponds, all linked to the Pallikaranai marsh. It is plagued by concerns like encroachments, sewage, solid waste pollution, and blocked canals. The charter has recommended a collective approach to tackle the concerns, instead of treating the lakes individually. Issues of various lakes Sathya Anand of the Saving Nanganallur Lake group said that the outlet channel completely disappears as the sewage starts entering the lake. In Velachery, Balakrishnan from the Tansi Nagar Welfare Association said that debris and encroachments interfere with water flow, and said that despite the court orders, the channel has not been fully restored. Atish Baisantry from the OMR Gandhinagar Plot Owners Welfare Association said that even though the Navallur lake has been restored, it lacks the sufficient outlet capacity. He added that construction has led to blocked natural waterways, which has caused flooding in the area. The charter calls for an independent, interdepartmental co-operative to examine the policies and to implement an exercisable plan. The charter was drafted after a consultation with the Pallikaranai Collective on June 20. The aim is to provide a common framework regarding the concerns raised about the watershed. This story was written by a student interning with TNM.

items.title: Times Now draws ire for recreating Manipur musician’s murder using AI, as family mourns
items.summary: On September 8, a Times Now show titled “Decoding Now”, which airs just before the primetime slot, ran a segment on Chongtham Vikram Singh, a 55-year-old Manipuri musician who was beaten to death outside his South Delhi home late on Sunday night. To illustrate what happened, the channel used a sequence of AI-generated clips. The clips included an AI-generated version of Singh confronting a group of youths outside his apartment; the youths chasing him; the mob assaulting him; and a bloodied man being carried down a staircase. It was captioned “Fists & Blows Rained on Vikram”. Other clips showed a bloodied victim lying in front of his apartment door, being carried down the stairs in a blood-stained T-shirt by a character who is presumably a family member, and then carried into an ambulance. All these clips ran under banners like “Delhi Hangs Its Head In Shame”, “Manipuri Musician Murdered” and “What Killed: Racism or Rage?” as anchor Meghna Deka and panellists Ponting Thokchom of the North East Students’ Society and journalist Subir Bhaumik discussed the tragedy. Many users on social media called out the channel for airing AI-generated clips depicting a murder and urged them to spare a thought for the grieving family. Pawan Khera, Rajya Sabha MP from the Congress party, tweeted: “There is nothing responsible or journalistic about turning a real person’s violent death into manufactured television imagery. items.title: Karnataka to sing only 2 stanzas of Vande Mataram at state events
items.summary: The Karnataka government, on September 9, ordered that only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram be recited at state government events. All six stanzas of the national song will be recited at events attended by the President of India, Prime Minister, or Governor of Karnataka. The order read, “The Ministry of Home Affairs has issued guidelines regarding the official version of the National Song ‘Vande Mataram’ and its singing or playing at various government and public functions to be followed on a case-by-case basis.” The Union government’s guidelines specify the occasions related to playing and mass singing of the national song separately. “The Government has considered the need to maintain uniformity, respect and proper etiquette in the playing/singing of the national song ‘Vande Mataram’ in accordance with the nature and context of various government programmes and ceremonies held in the State,” read the order, which saidat the decision was made after discussion in the Cabinet. The singing of Vande Mataram had become the subject of much controversy recently, after the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Act, 2026 was passed by Parliament in July. The Amendment extends the same statutory protection to Vande Mataram as that enjoyed by the national anthem, ‘Jana Gana Mana’, and stipulates punishment of up to three years' imprisonment for desecration of or disrespect towards the national song. In a July 9 order, the Union Ministry of Home Affairs, said that the official version of Vande Mataram contains six stanzas, including four controversial stanzas that are considered to be communally-charged.

items.title: After 37 years, Karnataka to bring back student elections in colleges
items.summary: After a 37-year gap, student elections will return to colleges and universities in Karnataka from the 2026-27 academic year, marking a historic return of campus democracy in the state. The Karnataka Cabinet has approved the reintroduction of student union elections, which were banned in 1989-90 following a series of violent incidents and clashes in educational institutions during the tenure of then Chief Minister Veerendra Patil. The elections, however, will not be mandatory. Deputy Chief Minister G Parameshwara said college managements will have to conduct elections if students want them, but cannot hold them if students choose not to. “If students don't want it, they can decide not to have it. The management cannot decide. It is the students' choice,” he said. The government has also decided that political parties and student organisations cannot contest the elections under their banners. Candidates must be enrolled students of the institution where they are contesting. Students who are members of political or student organisations can contest, Parameshwara said, provided they do so independently. “Candidates who are members of student organisations can contest as long as they do not do it under the banners of student political groups,” he said. Under the proposed structure, each student union will have a president, two vice-presidents, a general secretary, two joint secretaries and a six-member executive committee. One vice-president, one joint secretary and two executive committee positions will be reserved for women. The Cabinet has decided against caste-based reservations in student unions. Parameshwara said the government did not want to encourage caste-based elections among students. The decision follows the recommendations of a Cabinet sub-committee headed by Medical Education Minister Sharan Prakash Patil. The committee visited colleges and universities before submitting its report, which formed the basis for the Cabinet’s decision. The revival of student elections had been announced in the Karnataka government’s 2026-27 Budget. The elections will initially cover degree and pre-university colleges and universities, while schools will remain outside their scope. Student elections have been absent from Karnataka’s campuses since 1989-90, when the government banned them amid concerns over violence and clashes between student groups. items.summary: One would not be surprised to find that Dalits form the overwhelming majority of the thousands of ‘Pourakarmikas’ in what is now called the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA). A major section of them are also Dalit women. The official Kannada term for their occupation is a cover for its horrors. ‘Poura’ means city or civic, and ‘karmika’ means worker. According to the Karnataka Municipal Corporations Act, 1976, Pourakarmika means “a person employed in collecting or removing filth, in cleansing drains or slaughter-houses or in driving carts used for the removal of filth excluding night soil”. Recently, a video of GBA Minister and Vokkaliga leader Krishna Byre Gowda interacting with Pourakarmikas went viral and drew widespread cheers from his supporters. In this minute-and-a-half monologue, the Minister is seen responding angrily to drivers and helpers working in garbage vehicles who requested him to regularise their employment. Gowda’s diatribe needs quoting at some length to help readers take in the full import of his words as well as the feudal and casteist mindset behind it. Here’s one: “Why should we make you permanent when you are not even interested in coming for work? Instead of asking for permanency, you all should learn to work first. You all have learnt words to speak; instead, first learn to work.” How does this sound: “Those who have been made permanent do not come to work, and we cannot even question them. The city is stinking, and we have to face the abuses. You have nothing else except this. Do you have the thought of doing your work faithfully? Yes, you say; those are only words”. Here’s another: “You must have little humanity. You must have the intention to exert your labour when you wake up in the morning. You see this area and find that it is stinking.
